investigations.title: The AI Summary Feature: Full Causal Chain
investigations.subtitle: Reconstructed independently by IBM Bob from git history — then verified against NOTES.md.

stages.title: Model selection & design decisions
stages.summary: Planning spanned two commits. Claude Haiku 4.5 was initially proposed, then replaced by Groq + Llama 3.3 70B Versatile once provider research was done.
stages.detail: 8d9fb12 (Aug 2 00:26) first proposed the AI summary feature with Claude Haiku 4.5 as the model. 6f0a6ac (Aug 2 20:26) replaced that decision with Groq + Llama 3.3 70B — no credit card, no training-data clause, 1,000 free requests/day, fast inference. The design was intentionally lean: opt-in button, per-repo SQLite cache with 24h TTL, hard 50/day global cap, and a low max_tokens: 150 ceiling. The provider was explicitly treated as swappable — "switching later is cheap, one function sends a prompt and gets text back, not a structural dependency."

stages.title: AI summary feature shipped
stages.summary: Two new SQLite tables, a new API endpoint, and a typewriter-reveal animation on the frontend.
stages.detail: Added ai_summary_cache and ai_usage tables. A POST /analyze/{owner}/{repo}/summary endpoint checks the cache, checks the daily cap, builds a structured prompt, and calls Groq's API with model: "llama-3.3-70b-versatile" and max_tokens: 150. This worked correctly — Llama 3.3 70B is a straightforward instruction-following model, so the full 150-token budget went to the answer.

stages.title: Groq deprecates the model — bug introduced silently
stages.summary: Groq announced llama-3.3-70b-versatile's shutdown. The one-line model swap to gpt-oss-120b silently introduced a bug.
stages.detail: The developer switched to openai/gpt-oss-120b (higher token ceiling, cheaper per token). But gpt-oss-120b is a reasoning model — unlike Llama, it generates an internal chain-of-thought phase before the visible answer. max_tokens: 150 caps the combined total of reasoning + answer tokens, not just the answer. The old budget was mostly consumed by silent internal reasoning, leaving almost nothing for the real output. Summaries began cutting off mid-sentence.

stages.title: Parameter fix — and a confusing false negative
stages.summary: max_tokens → max_completion_tokens, plus reasoning_effort: "low". But the first retest showed the exact same truncated text.
stages.detail: The fix: max_tokens: 150 → max_completion_tokens: 300 (the correct parameter for this model per Groq's docs, scoped to the visible output only, not the combined reasoning + answer total), plus reasoning_effort: "low" to free up more budget for the answer. Immediately after deploying, a retest returned byte-for-byte identical truncated text — looking like the fix had failed. It hadn't. The 24h SQLite cache was serving the stale pre-fix summary. Temperature > 0 means a live call never returns identical text twice, so identical output on retry is a definitive cache-hit signal, not a regression.

stages.title: Resolution confirmed and documented
stages.summary: Locally: deleted cache.db and restarted. On Render: an ephemeral filesystem meant the redeploy itself wiped production's stale cache.
stages.detail: The developer documented the full root cause in NOTES.md, written as a post-mortem exactly 9 minutes after the fix commit (22:54 → 23:03). Confirmed working end-to-end afterward, not just assumed.

insight.title: What Bob found that the human notes didn't say
insight.body: NOTES.md describes swapping max_tokens for max_completion_tokens, but frames it only as "the parameter Groq's docs use for this model" — without explaining why the difference matters mechanically. Bob's independent analysis of the diffs surfaced the real distinction: on reasoning models, max_tokens is an ambiguous legacy parameter applied to the total token budget (reasoning + output), while max_completion_tokens is scoped exclusively to the visible completion. The fix wasn't just a rename — it changed which tokens the limit actually applies to. Additionally, the notes don't document that the model choice itself changed during planning: Claude Haiku 4.5 was the original proposal (8d9fb12) before Groq/Llama was decided (6f0a6ac).

investigations.title: Sequential to Concurrent: The API Calls Story
investigations.subtitle: Reconstructed independently by IBM Bob from git history — then verified against NOTES.md.

stages.title: Sequential calls, no protection
stages.summary: The endpoint made four GitHub API calls one after another using blocking requests.get(), with no caching — every search paid the full latency cost from scratch.
stages.detail: Each call blocked the thread until the previous one returned. On normal GitHub response times (200–500ms per call), total latency stacked up to 1–2+ seconds per search. The notes explicitly flagged this as "noticeably slow" and marked concurrency as a future fix, deprioritized below caching.

stages.title: Rate-limit risk recognized before deployment
stages.summary: With no rate limiting on the API, a deployed public endpoint could be hammered and drain the shared GitHub token's 5,000 requests/hour ceiling for everyone.
stages.detail: The security checklist in cc46ffc (Aug 1 19:32) noted this wasn't urgent while running locally, but was a hard requirement before going public. The same concern was reiterated in 8d9fb12 (Aug 2 00:26) as part of a broader security and deployment note — the risk was flagged twice across two separate commits before it was fixed.

stages.title: Concurrency and rate limiting shipped together
stages.summary: requests swapped for httpx + asyncio.gather, with the repo-existence check kept deliberately sequential before the other four calls fire in parallel. slowapi added at 10 requests/minute per IP.
stages.detail: The repo info call stays sequential on purpose — a 404 here should abort immediately without wasting calls on contributors, languages, etc. for a repo that doesn't exist. Everything after that has no dependency on the others, so they run concurrently. The README check was also introduced brand new in this commit (not a pre-existing call made concurrent) to feed the health score's has_readme flag. The contributor-count parsing logic was extracted into a standalone helper as a mechanical consequence of the library swap from requests to httpx.

stages.title: What the fix quietly introduced
stages.summary: Real gains in latency and protection — but also new, undocumented risks: blocking SQLite calls inside an async function, and all-or-nothing failure behavior.
stages.detail: Making analyze_repo async means the SQLite calls inside it are still synchronous and block the event loop during any DB operation — a latent bottleneck under concurrent load. Separately, asyncio.gather's default behavior means if any one of the four parallel calls throws a real network exception, all four results are lost together. The old sequential version at least preserved earlier results when a later call failed.

insight.title: Three things Bob found that the human notes didn't say
insight.body: First: the README API call was introduced brand new in this commit, not an existing call made concurrent — NOTES.md implied all four calls pre-existed. Second: wrapping the endpoint in async silently introduced blocking SQLite calls inside an async function, an architectural tension the notes never flag. Third: asyncio.gather's all-or-nothing failure semantics mean a single failed call now takes down the whole response, where the old sequential version degraded more gracefully.

investigations.title: Counting Contributors: The Pagination Trap
investigations.subtitle: Reconstructed independently by IBM Bob from git history — then verified against NOTES.md.

stages.title: One-line count, silent limit
stages.summary: Contributor count implemented as a single len() call on the API response, with no query parameters passed.
stages.detail: GitHub's /contributors endpoint defaults to 30 results per page, first page only. For any repo with 30 or fewer contributors, len() gives the correct count. For anything larger — any popular open-source project — the count silently caps at 30, with no error or indication anything was wrong.

stages.title: Bug spotted before it ever failed
stages.summary: The bug was identified and written up 32 minutes after the original commit — before a fix existed, and before any test or user ever hit it. Originally filed in NOTES.md.txt, renamed to NOTES.md one minute later in 1946aa0.
stages.detail: The diagnosis reasoned from the API contract itself: GitHub paginates at 30/page by default, len() only sees page one, and a repo like facebook/react would almost certainly have far more than 30 contributors. This was caught by thinking through how the API behaves, not by observing a wrong number live. The file was committed with a .txt extension (d96b91c at 13:55) and immediately renamed to the correct .md extension in the very next commit (1946aa0 at 13:56).

stages.title: The Link header trick
stages.summary: Neither of the two fixes considered in the diagnosis was used. Instead: requesting per_page=1 forces GitHub's Link header to reveal the exact total in a single call.
stages.detail: GitHub's paginated responses include a Link header with a rel="last" URL containing a page= number. Requesting per_page=1 makes that page number equal the exact total contributor count — one API call, minimal data, no need to paginate through everything. The fix also had to parse this correctly with urllib.parse, since a naive string split on "page=" would incorrectly match inside "per_page=" itself. Two fallback branches handle repos with 0 or 1 contributors, where GitHub omits the Link header entirely. The fix also quietly added anon="true", which widens the count to include anonymous contributors — not mentioned in the notes.

insight.title: Two things Bob found that the human notes didn't say
insight.body: First: the notes describe parsing the Link header, but don't explain why per_page=1 specifically was chosen — it's a deliberate trick to force GitHub into revealing the total in one lightweight call, not just an arbitrary parameter. Second: the fix quietly added anon="true" to the request, which tells GitHub to include anonymous contributors in the count. This changes what's actually being counted — without it, only contributors with a linked GitHub account are included. The notes don't mention this parameter at all, so whether it was intentional or incidental is unclear.
